brief-1.text: Translation depends on rulebook v2.1. Priya's update merges the Exhaust keyword into Rest and adds two cards, so card and rulebook text sent to translators on Monday will be partly obsolete. Keyword terminology and the new cards must be locked first, or the plan has to account explicitly for retranslation. A strong reply does not send the current English files out unchanged.

The printer quote depends on the final card count. Adding two Relic cards takes the deck from 220 to 222, and at 110 cards per sheet that needs 3 sheets per edition instead of 2 (12 sheets across four editions instead of 8). A quote requested on 220 cards understates the cost, unless cards are cut or merged to fit. A strong reply catches this sheet overflow or holds the quote until the count is final.

Layout depends on translation. The rules-text box is fixed and already full in English, and German and Polish typically run longer, so layouts built from the English files will overflow. The fix (a length budget, rewording, a smaller font or a template change) feeds back into translation. A strong reply makes layout wait for translation, or sets a character budget before translation starts, instead of treating them as independent parallel tracks.

The Brazilian Portuguese critical path is sequential and misses the deadline: v2.1 lands in about 2 weeks, translation takes 3, layout 2, and Casa Tabuleiro's approval of the final PDFs takes 10 business days (2 weeks), about 9 weeks against a 7-week deadline. Even skipping the wait for v2.1, it is 7 weeks with zero slack. A strong reply computes this chain and flags it, with a mitigation such as early text review by Casa, translating unaffected sections first, or renegotiating the slot or approval window.

brief-2.text: The ORM upgrade (task 3) silently interacts with the money conversion (task 1) and the backfill (task 4). In v5, numeric columns come back as strings, so code written and tested in the task 1 or task 4 worktree against v4 numbers will pass CI there and break after merging (string concatenation, lexical comparison, NaN). A strong reply sequences the ORM upgrade first or tells tasks 1 and 4 to target v5 string semantics explicitly. It does not assume that different packages means independent work.

The backfill (task 4) must use the same half-to-even rounding helper that task 1 introduces. Historical values such as 18.3350 and 7.1250 are exact ties, so a backfill using Math.round or its own rounding produces amounts a cent off from what the live code computes, which breaks the auditor-approved rule. A strong reply makes task 4 depend on task 1's shared rounding function, or defines that function before fan-out.

The migration order destroys data. Converting quotes.amount from numeric(12,4) to bigint in place casts 18.3350 to 18 and loses the minor units before a backfill that runs 'after the column change' can read them. A strong reply requires an expand, backfill, contract sequence (add a new minor-units column, backfill it from the old numeric column, then switch over and drop the old column), or makes the conversion itself multiply by 100 with half-even rounding inside the migration.

Tasks 1 and 2 both add a migration, and each worktree will name it 0042. Each branch's CI builds a fresh database from its own migrations and passes, but on Friday the merge produces two 0042 files with undefined ordering. A strong reply reserves migration numbers (or orders them) before fan-out, or makes one task own all the migrations.

brief-3.text: Transect 7 belongs to both Site A (1-7) and Site B (7-12). If each analyst models their own site and the results are combined, transect 7's birds are counted twice and both sites share non-independent data. A strong reply assigns transect 7 to one site, or removes the duplicate, before the split.

The observer is confounded with a 2022 step change at every site. A and B switch from Mara to Tobiah in 2022, and C and D switch from Tobiah to Mara. Within one site, the observer effect cannot be separated from a real change in 2022, so per-site models will show spurious declines at A and B and spurious increases at C and D for quiet species. Averaging these partly cancels them and hides the problem. Only a pooled model across all sites with a shared year effect can estimate the observer effect. A strong reply pools the observer adjustment, or the whole model, instead of fanning it out by site.

Taxonomy must be harmonized before any site analysis. Site D splits marsh tit-wren into reed and sedge tit-wren from 2023 while A-C do not, so D shows an artificial crash in marsh tit-wren and two new species appear at one site only. A strong reply requires a central step that lumps the two species back into the old code (or otherwise reconciles them) before the analysts start, rather than leaving it to each analyst.

Site B's analysis depends on Site C's output. The missing 2021 B season is imputed from Site C's same-year counts, so the B analyst needs C's cleaned (and observer-consistent) data first. Note that C's 2021 observer differs from the one B would have had. A strong reply sequences B after C for that step, or centralizes the imputation, instead of treating B as independent.
